analysis:
The PR is documentation only. It adds one paragraph to docs/reference/protocol-messages.md (head lines 757-765), under `inference_response_chunk`. The paragraph says streamed `auto` tool calls span several chunks whose `choices[].delta.tool_calls` entries share one `index`. The first chunk carries `id`, `type`, `function.name` and an empty `function.arguments`. Later chunks carry only `index` and an arguments fragment, and consumers concatenate the fragments by `index`. All other calls are one complete entry. The paragraph cites `MLXOpenAIService.swift` `streamChatCompletionFrames`; that source is not supplied here, so the described behavior is not verified against code.

This changes no code, wire field, key, encryption, attestation, authorization or trust-grant behavior. It adds no new message type and no new field in the `EncryptedPayload` envelope. The sealed per-chunk path (T-008) is untouched: `data` is still empty when E2E encryption is active and `encrypted_data` carries the payload. Tool-call fragments live inside the decrypted SSE chunk body. They are provider-authored output, so a malicious provider could emit malformed or adversarial fragments (T-007 class). The consumer-side concatenation rule is the same trust boundary that already exists, and it is not made weaker by a doc line.

Two things to watch in integration. First, the coordinator or consumer must tolerate fragment streams where indexes are inconsistent or arguments are unbounded. That behavior is not in scope here and its implementation is outside the supplied evidence. Second, the code that streams tool-call fragments (the Swift server) may change the output-chunk shape, so the platform-owned parsing contract should be checked. I found no regression or threat-model gap from this diff. The base units for the surrounding file (lines 584-1451) were reviewed and contain no changed lines.
